mechanism: HELM imposes a fixed cross-product structure: every model is evaluated on every (scenario, metric) pair under standardized prompting conditions. This forces sparse prior evaluation coverage—where models shared few or no scenarios in common—to collapse into a dense, comparable matrix. Rankings then emerge from aggregating across all metrics simultaneously rather than a single accuracy score, exposing trade-offs that single-metric leaderboards hide by construction.
invariant: A model's apparent superiority is evaluation-protocol-relative: whenever only accuracy on self-selected benchmarks is reported, rankings are artifacts of selection bias rather than capability differences. Multi-metric, multi-scenario standardization is the invariant prerequisite for any cross-model comparison that claims generality.
prediction: Models that rank highly on accuracy-only leaderboards will show substantially different relative orderings when calibration, fairness, toxicity, and robustness are included as co-equal metrics. The model maximizing accuracy will not generally maximize the holistic aggregate, and the gap between the two rankings will widen as model count grows.
failure_mode: When the chosen scenario and metric set is itself unrepresentative—e.g., neglected English dialects and trustworthiness metrics are explicitly flagged as underrepresented—the dense benchmarking matrix yields false completeness: models appear holistically evaluated but systematic blind spots remain, making the standardized rankings misleading for deployment contexts those gaps cover.
source_excerpt: Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on a set of core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions.
